title: Module 15: Testing Pyramid, Assertions & Test Runners (All Chapters)
description: Comprehensive module-level assessment covering all chapters of Module 15: Testing Pyramid, Assertions & Test Runners.

cards.concept: Testing Pyramid Fundamentals & Test Runners: Node.js Native Test Runner (node:test)
cards.question: What advantage does Node's built-in `node:test` runner provide over external frameworks like Jest or Mocha?

options.text: It automatically rewrites code to Rust.
It runs natively with zero external dependencies, supports TypeScript/ESM out of the box, provides subtest concurrency, and emits standard TAP/spec output.
It executes tests directly inside production databases.
It replaces the need for write operations.

cards.explanation: Node.js native test runner (node:test) is built directly into the runtime, eliminating dependency overhead, supply chain attack surface, and transpilation setup.
cards.pitfall: Importing 'node:assert' instead of 'node:assert/strict' allows loose type coercion in assert.equal(), masking type mismatch bugs.

cards.concept: Testing Pyramid Fundamentals & Test Runners: Strict Assertions vs Loose Equality in Tests
cards.question: Why should tests strictly use `node:assert/strict` rather than legacy `node:assert`?

options.text: Legacy assert runs slower in CI environments.
`assert/strict` forces `assert.equal()` to behave like `assert.strictEqual()` (===), preventing false positive passes caused by loose type coercion.
Legacy assert throws exceptions on valid syntax.
Strict mode only works with CommonJS.

cards.explanation: In legacy assert, assert.equal(1, '1') passes due to == coercion. In assert/strict, assert.equal(1, '1') throws an AssertionError, enforcing strict type correctness.
cards.codeSnippet:
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
// assert.equal(1, '1'); // Throws AssertionError: 1 === '1'
cards.pitfall: Relying on loose assert matchers permits silent type regressions in API response tests.
